newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Fresh data boost German economic hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Fresh data boost German economic hopes.

text.p: The German government on Thursday stuck by its forecast that Europe's largest economy will grow by 2.5 percent in 1997, refusing to yield to the gloom that has reigned since unemployment surged last month.
"We are standing by our forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth," Rexrodt told parliament during a debate on the government's annual economic report.
"The German economy has been back on the growth track since the spring of 1996. All indications show that this will continue in 1997," he added.
The confident talk from Bonn coincided with positive January data from the respected IFO economics institute, which showed business confidence rising in Germany.

Meanwhile the Bundesbank said its main policy indicator, M3 money supply, grew at a faster-than-expected annualised rate in January, dampening the chances of an interest rate cut but showing the economy is well-provided with liquidity.
The Bundesbank left its interest rates unchanged at a policy meeting on Thursday, in line with expectations.

The items of favourable news -- particularly from Ifo -- formed a small bright point in a cloud of depression which has hung over Germany since unemployment surged to 4.7 million in January -- a level not seen since the 1930s.

The unexpectedly large growth in jobless queues triggered a wave of concern that Bonn's budgets could be so stretched that Europe's economic taskmaster could itself fail to reach the tough targets set for entry to the single European currency, due in 1999.
That in turn sparked a round of doom-ridden forecasts, taking the line that long-standing structural problems presented an unsurmountable barrier to German economic growth.

The worries were compounded by news last month that the German economy showed zero growth in the final quarter of 1996 from the third quarter, figures the Bundesbank updated on Thursday to show an even worse picture -- a small contraction of around 0.2 percent.

On Wednesday the central bank had warned Bonn that its forecast for a budget deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product this year left Germany perilously close to the three percent limit laid down for EMU entry in the monetary union's guiding Maastricht Treaty.
It urged Bonn to commit to more savings and to press ahead urgently with much-needed reforms of taxes and benefit systems to boost competitiveness and so create jobs.

But the sharp rise in the IFO institute's business climate index for west Germany -- to 93.3 from 90.9 -- gave new life to economists' hopes that solid economic growth this year could take some pressure off Bonn in its bid to keep its deficit low.
Juergen Pfister, senior economist at Commerzbank said, the IFO figure was much stronger than expected and proved that a downtrend in the figures late last year was only temporary.
March German government bond futures, buoyed for weeks by economic pessimism, reacted negatively, falling 0.20 point to 103.29.
Sonja Gibbs, a bond strategist at Nomura noted that both the IFO data and the January M3 figure, which showed annualised growth of 11.7 percent, were well above expectations.

"It shows that we do have a fairly strong cyclical recovery and we are seeing the effect of the weaker mark. I think we did expect sentiment to improve, we just didn't expect it for this particular month," she said.

Gernot Nerb, senior economist, at Salomon Brothers added: "This shows that the German economy is on track after a temporary weakness." But he said that he saw no reason to change his forecast for GDP growth of 2.25 percent in 1997.
Economists warned nonetheless that signs of improvement should not be used by Bonn as an excuse to relax on reform.
"The early indicators available do not send an all-clear signal to the political parties in Bonn," Trinkaus Capital Management warned in a commentary.

But the more positive data did send a signal to markets not to expect any further policy easing from the Bundesbank, analysts said, even though the Bundesbank's report this week played down the importance of a rise in January inflation.

Wholesale prices data on Thursday, which showed a sharp year-on-year rise to 1.2 percent in January from 0.3 percent in December, served as a reminder that January's consumer price rise of just 1.8 percent was still the highest in two years.
The statistics office, like the Bundesbank, blamed seasonal factors for the higher January costs.
